Aidan McAleenan and the congregation of St. Columba Catholic Church in North Oakland for hosting the annual Ceremony of the Crosses on New Year’s Eve. They are the lifelines to healing at the heart of the significant decline in homicides and shootings in Oakland in 2025. It is true. 2025 saw an approximately 20% reduction in homicides and shootings in Oakland. This is significant. We are headed in the right direction. While not a reason for rejoicing, it is a reason to applaud those people and programs, like Oakland Ceasefire, who are part of the needed efforts to reduce gun violence, reduce recidivism and help build healthy communities. It is also true that the over 60 homicides are over 60 too many. It is true that these deaths represent shattered families, grieving communities, searing trauma. They are reason for us to weep. The Oakland Ceasefire Partnership is committed to keep heading in the right direction in the year ahead. We would love to see a year in which no one dies from gun violence. Realistically, our goal for 2026 is a 10% reduction in shootings and homicides. While not a cause for rejoicing, it would mean a significant reduction in weeping. Let’s head in that direction. Rev. Hampton Field and Coaches’ Field will be closed from mid-December through mid-February as the City undertakes seasonal maintenance to restore heavily used natural turf and prepare the fields for spring use. Both fields have seen extensive wear from year-round activity, leaving bald spots and uneven surfaces. The maintenance work is designed to repair damaged areas and level worn sections to improve safety and playability. Crews will use slit-seeding and aeration to rehabilitate the turf. This process embeds seed directly into the soil, improving seed-to-soil contact and increasing the likelihood of successful germination. Hampton’s turf field will be fenced off during this period to prevent activity that could interfere with the work. Another key component of the project is fertigation, a method that delivers organic amendments and soil-building additives through the irrigation system. Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent explained the approach during a Nov. 5 presentation to the Parks Commission. “Precise micro-dosing through an irrigation system is a far more efficient method of amendment application than manual application,” Kent said. “Traditional topical fertilizing results in a lower product absorption, with Coaches’ Field (Photos courtesy of the city) a large amount of run-off. Constant micro application of organic-based nutrients increases soil and plant health.” The project also includes importing materials to address surface and soil conditions. Crews will add 25 cubic yards of Pac Bell cinders to the infield, a specialized mix once used at the San Francisco Giants’ field at Candlestick Park. An additional 75 cubic yards of sand will be applied to the outfields to fill low spots, improve aeration, and support reseeding. Kent noted that weather conditions play a critical role in the success of the work, particularly during the reseeding phase. Fields must be dry enough for tractors to operate safely, even as consistent moisture is needed for seed growth. “To perform re-seeding and germination, the field has to be dry enough for a tractor to navigate,” she said. “The upshot of this is that if rain slows down and we get a stretch where it’s dry enough to perform the work, then re-seeding will go on as planned. If it were to rain continuously throughout January, then we would simply not do re-seeding this year.” Although the fields will be closed during the maintenance period, the batting cages will remain open. City officials said recent rains have not set the project back, and both fields remain on track to reopen in February.

articles.text: Chief Teaching & Learning Officer, Exploratorium It’s 5 p.m., and it’s already growing dark outside. The holiday break is over, routines are settling back in, and everyone is feeling a bit cooped up. But here’s what I’ve learned over decades as an educator and a parent: winter’s early darkness isn’t something to simply endure. It’s an invitation. When the sun sets before dinner, we notice light differently. Suddenly, the glow of a streetlamp becomes fascinating. Shadows stretch across the living room floor. These aren’t distractions from learning. They are learning, happening in real time in the curious moments of daily life. This is the season when questions about light come naturally. Why does it get dark so early? Why do car headlights look different in the rain? Where do the colors in a rainbow come from? These wonderings are examples of thinking like a scientist, approaching the world with curiosity about the how and why. They invite us to pause, notice and explore. During these still-dark evenings, simple experiments with light become even more magical. Try creating a “Pixel Tube” with your kids. Roll strips of shiny Mylar or aluminum foil into small tubes, bundle them inside a larger tube made from construction paper, and add a wax paper screen on one end. When you look through it at different light sources, a lamp, a TV screen or holiday lights still up around the neighborhood, you’ll see pixelated, kaleidoscope-like patterns. It’s beautiful, and it’s also science in action, with light reflecting, bouncing and mixing in surprising ways. The genius of winter’s darkness is that it makes light more noticeable. In summer, we take brightness for granted. On a January evening, when a child aims a flashlight at the wall and discovers shadow puppets, or sees how light bends through a glass of water, they’re exploring how light works. They are watching it travel, reflect and refract, and interact with other materials in delightful ways. © The Exploratorium Visitors play at the Exploratorium’s iconic Colored Shadows exhibit, one of the museum’s most photographed experiences.

articles.text: Piedmont ranked No. 3 in NCS, No. 30 in State It was a busy end of December for the girls’ basketball team which heads into 2026 with a 9-2 overall record. The Highlanders recently reached the championship game of the 2025 SoCal Holiday Classic In San Diego from December 26-30, a tournament which brings together some of the top teams in California. Piedmont won opened with a 53-39 win over La Jolla Country Day, 75-36 against Santa Margarita in the quarterfinals, and edged out Iolani of Hawaii 48-46 in the semifinals. They advanced to the finals where they lost 55-48 to Brentwood School of Los Angeles. Jenelle Solis was named to the SoCal Holiday Classic’s All-Tournament team. She scored 51 points in the four games, to go along with 16 assists. Despite the title loss, Piedmont fought hard against a ranked team. Brentwood School enters the New Year ranked No. 34 in the State, while Piedmont is ranked 30th by MaxPreps, which dictates playoff seeding. Santa Margarita is No. 41, while La Jolla Country Day is No. 61. Piedmont looks ahead to the start of its Western Alameda County Conference schedule with a heated rivalry game against Bishop O’Dowd on January 13 at home in the Binks Rawlings Gym. It’s a game with league title and North Coast Section seeding implications, as O’Dowd comes in ranked No. 9 in NCS while Staff Photos Taylor White had 18 rebounds against Brentwood School and 16 rebounds against La Jolla Country Day. Savannah Dennig led scoring in the SoCal Holiday Classic finals with 17 points. Jenelle Solis earned All-Tournament honors at the SoCal Holiday Classic, which features top teams in California. Piedmont ranks No. 3. 55-48 loss in finals to Brentwood Piedmont trailed 22-15 to end the first quarter while both sides were even on scoring in each of the remaining three quarters. Piedmont and Brentwood each scored 13 points in the second quarter, 10 points in the third, and another 10 points in the fourth. Final stats: Savannah Dennig led with 17 points, seven rebounds, and three assists. Taylor White had 12 points, 18 rebounds, six assists, three steals, and a block. Solis had seven points, two assists, four rebounds, and a steal. Alexa Ba had six points and two rebounds. Andrea Martin had five points, five rebounds, two steals, an assist and block. 48-46 victory over Iolani Piedmont trailed 15-10 to end the first quarter but knotted things up by halftime, 25-25. The Highlanders took a narrow 40-39 lead in the third quarter, while they outscored ‘Iolani 8-7 in a low-scoring fourth quarter. Final stats: Martin led with 19 points, three rebounds, two assists, two steals, and three blocks. Solis had 15 points, six assists, two rebounds, and three steals. Ba had seven points and four rebounds. Dennig had four points, seven rebounds, three assists, and one steal. White had two points, seven rebounds, one assist, and one steal. Johnson had one point, three rebounds, and a block. 75-36 blowout of Santa Margarita Piedmont dominated the first quarter to make it 32-8 through the opening eight minutes. They extended the lead to 56-15 by halftime, while scoring 10 points in the third quarter and nine in the fourth. Final stats: Marin had 29 points, nine rebounds, two assists, five steals, and two blocks. Solis had 20 points, five assists, two rebounds, and two steals. Ba had 12 points, two rebounds, and a steal. Dennig had seven points, four rebounds, four assists, and two steals. White had four points, nine rebounds, nine assists, and two steals. Jaden Jones had three points and two rebounds. 53-39 win vs. La Jolla Country Day Piedmont got out to a 15-8 lead through the first quarter and extended the lead by one point in the second quarter to lead 29-21 by halftime. It was similar in the third with Piedmont outscoring La Jolla 12-11, leading 41-33 to start the final going. PHS added 12 points in the fourth, allowing seven. Final stats: Martin had 13 points, eight rebounds and two steals. White had 12 points, 16 rebounds, three assists, and four steals. Dennig had 10 points, seven rebounds, six assists, and three steals. Solis had nine points, one rebound, and three assists. Ba had nine points and six rebounds. articles.text: Dillon Casey scores career-high against Redwood Christian Staff Photos Dillon Casey scored a career-high of 35 points in Piedmont’s win over Redwood Christian. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team started 2026 in a strong way with two wins at Binks Rawlings Gym to stretch its winning streak to four games. They most recently beat Redwood Christian 57-51 with a comeback on Monday, January 5 and beat McKinleyville 65-50 on Saturday, January 3. articles.text: In a short video, the people behind Piedmont’s everyday services share highlights from the past year and what they mean for the community: https://tinyurl.com/4p6bmv7f Featured highlights of the video include: Access & community support • New online services: Community members can now file, search, and monitor Public Records Requests online. Members can register or renew a business license anytime, day or night, from the convenience of their homes. • Expanded after-care options: When school returned this fall, PRD launched “The Hangout,” a new after-school option designed to meet the needs of older elementary students. • Linda Beach Tot Lot: In November, this popular playground re-opened as Piedmont’s first inclusive-play tot lot, with improved ADA access and new equipment designed for children of all abilities. Safety & resilience • New 9-1-1 Dispatch Center: Piedmont’s most significant public safety investment in decades, the new Dispatch Center strengthens emergency response capabilities and positions the City for the next generation of 9-1-1 technology while delivering a major infrastructure upgrade to the Police Department, including secure, independent power with dedicated backup. • Community wildfire evacuation exercise: Residents in the Blair/Scenic neighborhood practiced evacuation alongside first responders, while dozens of Piedmonters joined in at home, conducting evacuation decision-making with their families using our video guide. Infrastructure, sustainability & planning for the future • Moraga Canyon Specific Plan: In October, after more than two years of public discussion, the City Council adopted a vision and implementation plan for a new neighborhood in Moraga Canyon – grounded in what community members value most. The Specific Plan provides a framework for future development that prioritizes wildfire resilience and improvements to pedestrian, bicycle, and traffic safety, while creating opportunities for more people to call Piedmont home. • Piedmont’s first green infrastructure: At Grand and Fairview, a new landscaped bioswale now captures and filters stormwater through native plantings, cleaning runoff before it drains to the Bay. • Greening the City fleet: This year, the City added two e-bikes, a low-speed electric utility vehicle, and a fully electric closed-circuit TV van used for sewer inspections, which helped reduce emissions in day-to-day operations. Looking ahead to 2026 In 2026 the city will open the new community pool, install new swings in Piedmont Park, install a memorial to Sidney & Irene Dearing at Triangle Park, and take the next steps to begin implementing the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan – all alongside the ongoing work that keeps essential services running smoothly every day.

Berkeley Repertory Theatre will host a four-day festival of solo performance work by formerly incarcerated artists next week, marking the culmination of a three-year residency by the Formerly Incarcerated People’s Performance Project (FIPPP). The festival will take place Thursday, January 15, through Sunday, January 18 at Berkeley Repertory’s Roda Theatre. It celebrates the completion of FIPPP’s tenure as the theatre’s first-ever company-in-residence, a partnership that began in 2023. Founded six years ago, FIPPP develops and presents solo performance stories by formerly incarcerated people with the aim of fostering understanding and social change through personal storytelling. The organization produced festivals in Oakland in 2021 and 2023 before joining Berkeley Repertory Theatre. It has since grown into a full-scale theatre company with eight professional directors and 15 formerly incarcerated artists. The festival will feature five distinct programs presented over four days. Each show includes multiple solo performances, as well as short documentary films by filmmaker Jim Granato that complement the live work onstage. Three of the performances will conclude with panel discussions featuring the performers, offering audiences an opportunity to engage more deeply with the material. The conversations will be moderated by Bay Area theatre artists Dan Hoyle, Wayne Harris and Mark McGoldrick, all of whom also serve as coaches with FIPPP. Twelve formerly incarcerated performers will appear in the festival, bringing diverse backgrounds that include stand-up comedy, TEDx talks, The Moth storytelling competitions, Shakespearean theatre and appearances at the San Francisco Fringe Festival. Their stories explore paths to incarceration, life inside prison and the challenges of reentry, shaped and directed by FIPPP’s professional creative team. For more information, visit https://fippp.org/.

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum’s newest exhibition, Rave into the Future: Art in Motion, is on view now through January 26, 2026. The exhibition spotlights women and queer artists from the West Asia diaspora currently based in the United States and Europe and is inspired by West Asian rave and underground music culture. Oakland-based Arab Persian American artist Sahar Khoury contributes a multimedia sculpture equipped with a functioning DJ deck that will be activated by local Asian and Asian diaspora DJs. Los Angeles–based Yemeni American artist Yasmine Nasser Diaz’s installation For Your Eyes Only recreates an intimate bedroom where projections of dancers, archival clips, and protest materials form a layered portrait of generational expression and activism. Disguise as Dancefloor, a nearly 100-square-foot copper dancefloor by London-based Lebanese American artist Joe Namy, is designed to record the footsteps of visitors while symbolizing the healing properties associated with the material across cultures. Other featured pieces bring humor, futurism, and fantastical narrative into the mix, including Meriem Bennani’s Party on the CAPS, Sophia al Maria and Fatima al Qadiri’s bass-driven Spiral, and Farah Al Qasimi’s horror-comedy Um Al Naar. The exhibition culminates in a glitter-filled “after-party” animated by robotic vacuum cleaners in Puff Out by the Brussels-based duo :mentalKLINIK. Curated by Naz Cuguoğlu, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art, the exhibition has already earned significant recognition. Cuguoğlu received a curatorial research fellowship from The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts last year, and the museum was recently awarded an additional foundation grant to bring the project to fruition. “I wanted to create a space for narratives that build solidarity through joy, pleasure, and laughter,” Cuguoğlu said, noting the need to counter dominant Western portrayals of West Asia rooted in Orientalism and suffering. “This exhibition asks what we can learn from the autonomy, healing, and bliss that unfold on the dancefloor,” Cuguoğlu said. Museum Director and CEO Soyoung Lee added that the show offers a timely opportunity to broaden public understanding of West Asia while celebrating the universal joy of collective dance. Rave into the Future: Art in Motion is on view at the Asian Art Museum now through January 26, 2026.

articles.text: The San Francisco Botanical Garden in Golden Gate Park hosts a free birdwatching tour the first Sunday of every month, guided by members of the Golden Gate Bird Alliance. Golden Gate Bird Alliance is a nonprofit organization dedicated to the conservation of birds, wildlife and their habitats in the San Francisco Bay Area. Founded in 1917 and formerly known as the Golden Gate Audubon Society, the group works to engage the public through education, advocacy and hands-on activities such as free bird walks, habitat restoration and community science projects. Its mission is to inspire people to protect Bay Area birds and the shared natural environment, and its programs span birding outings, speaker events and youth education. Based in Berkeley, the organization serves San Francisco, Oakland and surrounding communities, aiming to foster a broad conservation community and support long-term habitat stewardship across the region. Every month, members visit the San Francisco Botanical Garden to offer a free, community bird-watching tour. The event, entitled “Birding at the Garden,” invites birdwatchers of all ages and skill levels to attend. Attendees are encouraged to bring their own binoculars and a water thermos. The next event is held on Sunday, February 1, between 8 a.m. and 11 a.m. Attendees meet at the Botanical Garden front gate. Registration will open one week before the scheduled walk, on Sunday at 8 a.m. Heavy rains cancel the event. To register, visit https://gggp. org/event/birding-at-the-garden-with-golden-gate-bird-alliance-16/. The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) is marking its 20th anniversary with Continuum: MoAD Over Time, an exhibition examining the museum’s history, on view now through March 1. Continuum presents a chronological and thematic overview of MoAD’s development from its founding to the present, while also addressing its future direction. The exhibition features archival materials, fine art, interviews and community narratives that document the museum’s impact on arts education, cultural programming and public engagement, as well as its artistic influence in the Bay Area and beyond. Exhibition highlights include materials related to long-running initiatives such as the museum’s Emerging Artist Program and “MoAD in the Classroom,” as well as community events including the Afropolitan Ball and Diaspora Dinner. These elements illustrate how the institution has supported artists of the African Diaspora and expanded access to cultural resources over two decades. Continuum includes works by Cheryl Patrice Derricotte, Chester Higgins Jr., JoeSam., Richard Mayhew, Ramekon O’Arwisters, Gordon Parks, Lava Thomas and Sam Vernon. articles.text: Exhibition leaves Jan. 25 Art of Manga is on view now at de Young, featuring over 600 drawings by more than a dozen iconic Japanese artists, comics and novelists who specialize in the genre. Manga, a type of imagedriven narrative storytelling in Japan, has become widely popular in Western culture over the last two decades. The de Young is the first North American museum to highlight Manga and its prominent, modern-day artists in a major exhibition. Featured artists include Chiba Tetsuya, Akatsuka Fujio, Takahashi Rumiko, Taniguchi Jiro, Yamazaki Mari, Araki Hirohiko, Yamashita Kazumi, Tagame Gengoroh, Yoshinaga Fumi, Oda Eiichiro, and Tanaami Keiichi. “Captivating millions around the world with dynamic graphic narratives, manga is one of the most significant visual mediums of our time,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “San Francisco has long been a gateway for Japanese cultural exchange in the United States, and we are delighted to honor this legacy by showcasing the artistry and power of contemporary Japanese narrative art in Art of Manga.” Art of Manga organizing curator Nicole Coolidge Rousmaniere said the genre cultivates “an ease of visceral understanding that enables readership from around the world.” “We are living in a time when the narrative shift from text to images is increasingly becoming a reality,” she added. “Readers become invested in characters and their stories, and manga publishers and artists take their letters and social media comments into account and adapt the ongoing story or create new manga, which often then becomes a forerunner to greater cultural shifts.” Art of Manga is on view at de Young museum now through January 25, 2026. For more information, visit https://www.famsf.org/. Photo courtesy of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco Museum patrons view the Art of Manga exhibition at de Young.

articles.text: Recently, a Post reader asked whether the paper would again review or critique newly released feature films: those that still open in familiar walk-in movie theaters. The question was born of observation and curiosity. Yet something has clearly changed, not only at the Post but also in this century-old form of entertainment and the venues that have long defined it. This raises two related questions: What is happening, and what does it mean? In thinking about this, I searched for an analogue; something equally transformative, even revolutionary. I settled on Johannes Gutenberg, who around 1450 invented movable metal type, a compatible oil-based ink and a screw-down press. His first major work was reportedly the Bible. Before Gutenberg, copies of the Bible were painstakingly produced by hand. What his invention unleashed was an explosion of accessible knowledge and the broad sharing of information, leading to scientific inquiry, global exploration, and advances in architecture and philosophy. It marked a Renaissance of creativity, made manifest in the arts, including theater and literature, as well as in innovation. One could argue we now find ourselves in a similar period, a breathtaking technological renaissance that began in the early 1900s and continues today. Consider the telegraph; photography, including cameras and movie projectors; the automobile; the telephone; radio; flight; space travel; television; the computer; Wikipedia; the internet; email; smartphones; and more; a kaleidoscope of change. And now, artificial intelligence. Filmmaking, moving from celluloid to digital technology, has not been exempt. Hollywood content now streams on platforms such as Prime, Netflix and Disney+, among many others. As with books in the 1450s, this shift has produced an explosion of change: series, episodes and a new richness of character development for writers. For audiences, the change has meant access. A vast historical archive of films is now readily available. Will movies watched on high-tech, large screens at home prove transformative? Will walk-in theaters become relics of the past? Likely. composer Louise Farrenc. This composer has recently become a “cause célèbre”…musically speaking. Judging from the single movement it seems that Farrenc was inf luenced by both Beethoven and Mendelssohn. I hope that the orchestra will present Farrenc’s entire Symphony in the near future. Youthful virtuosity can be awe inspiring. While some important musicians of the past rejected youthful virtuosity, I am amazed by it. The soloist of the evening was the very young violinist Lisa Saito. Her performance was, in a word, amazing. Judging from her all-encompassing technique and rich tone, she has a promising future. Her vehicle of the evening was the monumental First Violin Concerto of Niccolo Paganini. While a few chronic mal-contents continue to downgrade Paganini, he was held in the highest esteem by superlative musicians like Rossini, Liszt, Chopin and Schumann. Rossini once said: “It is a very good thing that Paganini did not write operas because he would have eclipsed all of us.” Paganini was probably the most astonishing musician of all time. The world would be a poorer place if Paganini had not asserted his genius in all aspects of music and all aspects of publicity. As a musician, the Italians adopted the phrase “Paganini never repeats” to describe his unlimited imagination in music. If the young violinist Lisa Saito adds this aspect to her playing… Watch out. After intermission, the concert concluded with the entire Beethoven Symphony No. 7. As the concert proceeded, I observed the conductor carefully. Fankuchen is a real maestro. In many ways he resembles the renowned conductor Raphael Kubelik both on appearance and conducting style. He inspires his orchestra at all times and especially in the climactic phrases. After the concert, I spoke with a number of the musicians. They all agreed that Fankuchen is an inspiring musician, and they are happy to have him as their director. In this respect, he is the true inheritor of the conducting mantle of Edgar Braun. Edgar was the most generous and openminded musician I have ever met. Thanks to him, I had opportunities to present my first important concerts in San Francisco. The good memories remain. It was a perfect way to end the year.

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, January 7, 2026 Critic’s note: the only constant is change By Chris Honoré Recently, a Post reader asked whether the paper would again review or critique newly released feature films: those that still open in familiar walk-in movie theaters. The question was born of observation and curiosity. Yet something has clearly changed, not only at the Post but also in this century-old form of entertainment and the venues that have long defined it. This raises two related questions: What is happening, and what does it mean? In thinking about this, I searched for an analogue; something equally transformative, even revolutionary. I settled on Johannes Gutenberg, who around 1450 invented movable metal type, a compatible oil-based ink and a screw-down press. His first major work was reportedly the Bible. Before Gutenberg, copies of the Bible were painstakingly produced by hand. What his invention unleashed was an explosion of accessible knowledge and the broad sharing of information, leading to scientific inquiry, global exploration, and advances in architecture and philosophy. It marked a Renaissance of creativity, made manifest in the arts, including theater and literature, as well as in innovation. One could argue we now find ourselves in a similar period, a breathtaking technological renaissance that began in the early 1900s and continues today. Consider the telegraph; photography, including cameras and movie projectors; the automobile; the telephone; radio; flight; space travel; television; the computer; Wikipedia; the internet; email; smartphones; and more; a kaleidoscope of change. And now, artificial intelligence. Filmmaking, moving from celluloid to digital technology, has not been exempt. Hollywood content now streams on platforms such as Prime, Netflix and Disney+, among many others. As with books in the 1450s, this shift has produced an explosion of change: series, episodes and a new richness of character development for writers. For audiences, the change has meant access. A vast historical archive of films is now readily available. Will movies watched on high-tech, large screens at home prove transformative? Will walk-in theaters become relics of the past? Likely. articles.text: Kiki’s Delivery Service, created by master storyteller and animator Hayao Miyazaki, who is regarded as the Walt Disney of Japan, was adapted from a popular Japanese coming-of-age novel by Author Eiko Kadono. It’s an extraordinary example of Studio Ghibli’s prodigious talents, incorporating fantasy and a benign crisis into a remarkable tale about a spunky young witch (never sinister) on the cusp of womanhood. Kiki, an adolescent witch, now 13, as tradition dictates, must leave home to complete her magic training in another town. She takes with her talking cat JiJi, a red radio, and hopes to practice her still rocky broom flying skills. She ends up lodging with a baker for whom she begins an airborne delivery service. Beautifully crafted, saturated with rich colors, the story touches on newbie teen issues such as independence, femininity, insecurity, friendship and even (unexpectedly for a children’s movie) sexuality, all in a warm, lighthearted manner. In essence, Kiki’s Delivery Service is a wonderful adventure; however, it is also a personal crossroads for Kiki, who, after an illness, loses her powers and must find a new purpose for her young life. The tale is consistently funny, optimistic, and exciting, finding and holding that coveted sweet spot that makes Miyazaki’s films simply exceptional. Kiki’s Delivery Service. Jeannie Anderson A: The housing market predictions seem to be fairly upbeat and positive, looking to be defined by a combination of items that can create a healthier and balanced market. Mortgage rates seem to have made an improvement and the buyers have come to accept the mid-6% range as tolerable. The softened condo market opens up first time home-buyer opportunities and mid-market prices overall this year will probably stay within a modest gain. Due to the tech-heavy Bay Area boom, cash buyers keep driving the higher end luxury market. The lack of inventory may start shifting as life circumstances will propel longtime homeowners to accept the financially painful aspect of moving and giving up the 3% loan. Another item to note as having an effect on inventory, if it passes in Congress, would be lower capital gains taxes for a personal residence sale — a big factor for 15-year-plus homeowners. This past year saw the real estate industry undergo some volatile changes, lawsuits, MLS rulings and this year’s possible Compass/Anytime merger. The outcomes are meant to improve the transactions for consumers, and add more transparency. Starting the next half of the decade with a stable market should help buyers and sellers in their endeavors. Jeannie Anderson Coldwell Banker Realty 415-271-4887 jeannie.anderson@cbrealty.com Jeremy Davidson A: In 2026, I expect the Bay Area market to be driven largely by necessity. Buyers and sellers who transact will do so because life compels them — a job change, partnering up, family growth, downsizing, or needing to be closer to aging parents. Those circumstances move people to action regardless of what rates are doing. And speaking of rates: yes, they’ll keep some buyers sidelined, but our market has never been typical. The prevalence of cash — fueled by tech equity, AI startup windfalls, and generational wealth — will keep transactions flowing, particularly at the upper end. Conversely, sellers sitting pretty with sub-4% mortgages won’t budge unless they’re decamping for a less expensive market or have enough to buy their next home outright. The AI boom and big tech expansions should persist, meaning jobs and capital will continue pouring into our region, propping up both rents and home prices, especially in the luxury tier. As for what buyers want? That hasn’t changed: turnkey properties close to great schools and neighborhood amenities. Sellers who invest not just in fresh paint and staging but in the bones — roof, foundation, water heater, electrical — will be best positioned. Today’s buyers don’t want a punch list waiting for them at the finish line. Jeremy Davidson Compass 415-717-4103 jeremy.davidson@compass.com DJ Grubb A: Market predictions need to be analyzed in our very different market segments. • First-time buyer market: Due to the cost of ownership, this market segment will continue to be very sluggish and will have very little — if any — appreciation over the next 12 months. The average age of the first-time buyer is now in their mid-30s and many young adults are literally opting not to be burdened by home ownership and would rather travel the world. • Mid market: A very awkward market segment due to the fact that the move-up buyer does not want to leave a sub-3% mortgage and the basic cost of living has accelerated so dramatically in the Bay Area. This segment of the market should continue to appreciate at a very conservative 5%, with maybe a bump if mortgage interest rates decline in the second quarter of the year. • High-end luxury market: This marketplace had a tremendous amount of momentum in 2025. This is very evident in sales volume, all-cash sales and the abundance of remodeling of significant larger homes. The rejuvenation of San Francisco and the new tech market push will maintain a very healthy luxury market in the Bay Area. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group says it never rains on Wednesday mornings in Piedmont, but there was a “very heavy mist” last Wednesday morning. It and this being New Year’s Eve reduced the group’s size. Eighteen water-resistant walkers and two of their K-9 best friends were on hand at the Exedra at their regular weekly gathering time. The Piedmont schools were still on their Holiday break and their campuses were open. Piedmont High, Piedmont Middle School, Millennium High School, and Havens Elementary were all in close proximity and a safe, short walk on a wet morning. Before they got started walking, some background school information was provided. The City of Piedmont was incorporated in September 1907. Since its population was growing dramatically after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, city leaders decided to build two schools to serve the community. The first school was built in 1910 and opened its doors in 1911. It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land donor. It turned out that Havens would be part of the high school’s history too. The walkers started off going behind the Exedra to a path along the top of the park that is a back, side entrance to the high school. They entered the campus and walked down a breezeway to covered area and some more PHS history was shared. In 1916 Havens was in big financial trouble. The Oakland Tribune reported lawsuits totaling $90,000 were filed against him. He had only a little land left from his fortune and it was in his wife’s name. The Anglo-California Trust Company held the mortgage on the Piedmont Park for $172,000, and neither the interest nor the principal had been paid. Havens had auctioned off his art collection and wanted to sell the park to raise funds. The Piedmont School Board voted to purchase some of the park for a new high school and athletic field. They wanted 13 acres, but Havens would not sell less than the park’s entire 27 acres. The City wanted to save the park from residential development but did not have money to purchase the remaining parkland, and in 1916 Piedmont voters defeated a measure to raise funds to buy the land. Havens died suddenly in 1918 from food poisoning. The parkland was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to purchase fourteen acres of the park in 1921 if the City would reimburse them, which it did in 1922 after a bond issue was approved by voters. This plan allowed the school district to buy the 13 acres it wanted and the City to have its park. Construction began immediately in 1921 on the high school. It was a reinforced concrete building with terra cotta trim for five hundred students. An auditorium spanned the front of the school with two stories of classrooms behind and two wings held more classrooms. Piedmont Junior High School and the athletic field were added in 1924, and other additions were built in 1937 and 1939. In 1974, the original school building was declared unsafe under state earthquake laws and was demolished. However, the demolition took longer than anticipated because the buildings were so well built that it was difficult to tear them down. Three new classroom buildings and a gymnasium were built, and the original library, quad, and administration buildings were rehabilitated. The new construction was done in the “back-to-nature” style that was then popular with a wood exterior. However, by the mid-2010s this construction was also deemed earthquake unsafe and these buildings had to be demolished too. The school was reconstructed and opened in the fall of 2021 with a new STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art, and Mathematics) building and a new theater after voters approved $56 million in bonds. Some more interesting facts were also shared. PHS girls were required to wear middy blouses and pleated skirts until the early 1960s. It was the last public school in California to resist pressure from the State to stop enforcing a dress code which required students, and specifically girls, to wear a uniform. The walkers admired the quad area in front of the Student Center and took a group photo. Then they walked over to Millenium High School (MHS) and talked about its history. The school was officially started in 2000 and named for the new millennium. It evolved from the school district’s previous alternative program, the Piedmont Independent Learning High School, that had opened in 1980. MHS has a small enrollment, usually around 60 students in grades 9 to 12. Classes are small, with about 10 to 20 students per class. A fun fact is that George Lucas, the creator of the Star Wars films, granted the school the right to use the image of the Millennium Falcon on school sweatshirts, as well as to represent it as its mascot, effectively creating the Millennium (High School) Falcon. Participating in last week’s Walking on Wednesdays were Jasmine Cai, Jim Kuo, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Mike Gallant, Denny McGee, Brian Hamlin, Mary Carter, Karen Palmer, Karin Fetherston, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Sherry Jacobs, Mark Davis, Dave DeRoche, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Jill and Ron Day were in from England visiting family and that Jing Jing Liu was walking with them for the first time.

articles.text: As the New Year begins, many people resolve to prioritize their health and well-being. For individuals living with disabilities, however, achieving wellness goals and carving out time for self-care can be far more challenging. Many disabilities are not visible, and people who live with them often assume they are less deserving of support than someone with an obvious impairment. That misconception can stand in the way of meaningful help. This is where service dogs can be life-changing. Trained to support individuals with both visible and invisible disabilities, service dogs increase independence, build confidence and improve overall quality of life. Their impact reaches far beyond companionship, offering daily, practical support that can make routine activities safer and more manageable. Service dogs offer benefits that extend beyond companionship, providing practical support for daily life. At a basic level, dogs provide unconditional love, which improves quality of life, reduces loneliness and supports better physical health. People who have dogs are more likely to get regular exercise, which research shows can be as effective as medication for those experiencing mild to moderate depression. Studies also indicate that petting a dog can lower heart and breathing rates, helping to reduce anxiety. Beyond the benefits of dog ownership in general, service dogs are trained to perform specific tasks that increase handler safety and comfort. Many people are familiar with mobility assistance, hearing alerts and guide dog work. Less visible, but equally important, are the tasks that support individuals with invisible disabilities such as post-traumatic stress disorder. These tasks can include deep pressure therapy for grounding and stress relief, panic attack mitigation, interruption of harmful behaviors, medication reminders and item retrieval. In addition, allergen and migraine alert tasks can dramatically improve a handler’s safety and sense of control. So how does someone take the first step toward prioritizing their well-being and beginning the serMissy, a psychiatric service dog, rides the train to support her handler’s invisible disability. vice dog training process? Some organizations breed and train dogs for specific handlers, while a growing number of service dog trainers work with existing pets to prepare them for service work. Although training typically takes six months or more and represents a significant financial investment, the long-term benefits often far outweigh the time and cost involved. Experts recommend reaching out to a local service dog trainer to learn more about the process. Because this is specialized work, it is important not to settle for just any dog trainer. Look for someone with experience training the specific tasks you need and who can provide references. Starting the process may feel daunting, but the New Year offers a natural moment to take a meaningful step toward better health. A service dog’s care, attentiveness and training have the potential to create a life-changing improvement. Putting your own needs first can be the beginning of a safer, more independent and more fulfilling year. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: The late Herb Stansbury was a meaningful contributor to Piedmont in many ways, not the least of which were his weekly cartoons, Dude, which appeared in the Piedmont Post from July 1999 until his passing on July 31, 2010.
